Strongly recommend learning Haskell. In principle it can be applied to any problem, but in reality it is still a niche product - but since one of the niches is the financial markets it can be a lucrative skill to have. Because Haskell is in some ways very close to the way mathematicians think, it is used by quants at some investment banks and hedge funds to write financial pricing software.

In my own work I use it mainly in statistical applications - it's possible to write very robust code very quickly, which always impresses people. Because Haskell is a functional programming language, learning it has also forced me to think more "functionally", and this has helped me develop very good habits in business analysis and system design.

You don't have to be particularly smart to learn Haskell, but you do have to be prepared to put in a bit of effort to get to a high standard. Most students learn enough in a college setting to understand the general principles, but don't commit enough time to fully understand "monads". Getting to grips with monads is, I suspect, what puts most people off Haskell. You need to practise using monads for a while, then suddenly the penny drops and you understand them. Most beginners don't do this, and I think this is what prevents them from becoming working Haskell programmers.

First off, I am completely nuts about Haskell. (Can you tell from my name?) I've been programming in Haskell for the last 3 years, and I've been developing in it full-time at my work for the past month (I've got an awesome project they're letting me start).

The key features of Haskell are purity, type-safety, concurrency, and native compilation.

I've developed in Python for 7 years and after I learned Haskell, writing Python became extremely frustrating. Not being able to have any control over the types that are passed to your functions or what types are returned by the functions you call made me paranoid. Strong+static types are like documentation that is enforced by the compiler. In dynamically typed languages, anything can be any type for seemingly no reason. Some people hear strong+static types and assume the verbosity of C++ and Java, but it's actually quite the opposite. Haskell's type interference means you only specify the types when you need to and let the compiler figure out the rest.

Types force you to make sure you've reasoned about your problem correctly. Type driven development (TDD) is a popular phrase. I find I don't need to write nearly as many test cases for Haskell because about 80% of my tests are type related in Python, and those cases are checked automatically by the compiler in Haskell. Almost daily I find when I need to make a big change, I tweak the types, I fix the compiler errors, and it just works.

I highly recommend Parallel and Concurrent Programming in Haskell to learn about Haskell awesome concurrency model.

Not having to deal with a run-time is great, though I wish Haskell's build tools were better (they're working on it, but it's a hard problem). "Cabal hell" will become a familiar phrase, but sandboxes and stackage are good way to mitigate it.

To answer your question more directly, Haskell is a general purpose language (just like Python and C++), which means there is nothing you can't build with it that you can't build in those other languages. Haskell starts feels like the best solution when building parsers and servers. I highly recommend learning parsec if you want to see where Haskell really shines. Web servers are another good introduction to Haskell usefulness. My go-to web server library is Spock.

If you're curious why Haskell isn't more popular despite these great benefits, the answer is because its different. Haskell is so alien from other languages that you really feel like you're starting from scratch as a developer when you're learning it (just like how programming felt when you wrote your first if-statement), but once you learn it, the concepts feel very natural. I consider experience in imperative languages to be a hindrance when learning Haskell because you'll be tempted to try to solve a problem the wrong way. A common mistake developers make is they try to port one of their imperative programs to Haskell, but they inevitably get flustered because the concepts are incompatible. Take a fresh approach and pretend you're learning programming for the very first time.

If you're still interested in Haskell, there are tons of Haskell talks on Youtube. I recommend watching some and seeing if anything sparks your interest.

idk, I haven't written any C++ since just before C++11. I do know Haskell has much stronger safety guarantees than C++ and I've found type-classes and Haskell's type system in general to be far superior to OOP. I highly recommend this post by Edward Kmett. If all you care about is type-interference then stick with C++.

Another exciting language is Rust, which borrows (teehee) some ideas from Haskell. I want to get familiar in it, but I rarely need/want that kind of low-level control. It is by far the most promising C++ killer.

There are not many jobs in Haskell. However, the thing about Haskell is that it will change how you write C++ and Python. Understanding why purity is useful changes how you look at object-oriented programs and makes you acutely aware of mutable state. Similarly, most Python programmers neglect list comprehensions and map(), even when they would provide a much more concise solution than a for loop. The type system also really opens your eyes to the deficiencies of those in other languages and provides you with new abstractions for thinking about problems.

Don't learn Haskell because it's useful in it's own right - learn it because it will change how you write code in general. (I've heard Lisp has some similar benefits, but I haven't learnt it yet myself.)
